clue.text: Mythical pusher, sister, remarkably pushy

indicators.note: remarkably suggests the letters of pushy are arranged in an unusual new way

explanation.surface: A legendary figure doing the pushing, described as a strikingly pushy sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remarkably' rearranges PUSHY into YPHUS, which follows SIS. The king in Greek myth was condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek king was punished in Hades by endlessly shoving a boulder up a hill, the archetypal mythical pusher.

clue.text: Take fruit to the rear in pursuit of science

indicators.note: following in pursuit puts the rear piece after the science piece

parts.note: SC is a standard abbreviation for science
the rump is the hindquarters, the rear

explanation.surface: Someone heading off to collect fruit, trailing after science.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in pursuit of' places RUMP after SC. To scrump is British slang for stealing apples from an orchard.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrumping is British slang for pilfering apples or other produce from orchards.

clue.text: Live off cake

explanation.surface: A note about surviving on nothing but cake.
explanation.definitionFit: To sponge is to scrounge from others for a living; a sponge is also a light airy baked dessert.

clue.text: Capital referee of beauty contest

explanation.surface: A city official judging a beauty pageant.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the Trojan prince chose between Hera, Athena and Aphrodite, awarding the golden apple to the fairest.
explanation.definitionFit: The French capital shares its name with the Trojan prince who judged the goddesses' beauty contest.

clue.text: Contrived clue "Socialist suffering sores"

indicators.note: something contrived is artificially put together, so the letters of clue are reworked

parts.note: red is the traditional colour and nickname for a socialist

explanation.surface: A setter's complaint about a forced clue for a left-winger in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contrived' turns CLUE into ULCE, then RED follows; the quotation marks are only dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: Being covered in open lesions or ulcers means suffering from sores.

clue.text: embraced a model and calmed down

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'embraced a model and calmed down' has lost its opening cross-reference (14, i.e. ABED, which wraps A + T); no clue word gives ABED as held
annotationWithheld.clue: embraced a model and calmed down

clue.text: Large animal's facial feature, note — and another

parts.note: the brow is the forehead, a feature of the face
another large animal, following on from the definition, gives a bear

explanation.surface: Describing a big creature by its face, with a footnote mentioning a second one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' points back to 'Large animal', so it supplies a second big beast, BEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: This hefty ursine species of Eurasia and North America is one of the biggest land carnivores.

clue.text: Striker's comment supplying advice to shoplifter'?

explanation.surface: A boxer's taunt doubling as a tip for a petty thief.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is said while landing a punch; the second reads the phrase literally as an instruction to steal an item.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation accompanies a blow; literally it is an order to pocket an item, which suits a thief.

clue.text: Let off school, having out side appointment

indicators.note: the appointment has the school inside it, its letters sitting on the outer side

parts.note: a date is an arranged appointment
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: A pupil released from school because of an outside appointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having out side' (printed as two words) means DATE goes outside ETON. ETON is the English boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: To let off a bomb or firework is to set it off, to explode it.

clue.text: Luggage-bearer loves to put father through torment

indicators.note: putting something through another piece places it inside

parts.note: the rack was an instrument of torture, so to rack is to torment
love is zero in tennis, and zero looks like O, so loves gives two Os
FR is the abbreviation for father, a priest's title

explanation.surface: Someone who loves to see Dad tortured, oddly linked to baggage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'through' puts OO and FR inside RACK, giving R + OOFR + ACK.
explanation.definitionFit: A frame fixed on top of a car carries suitcases and bags, bearing the luggage.

clue.text: Memento of philosopher and original thinker

parts.note: John Locke was the English empiricist philosopher

indicators.note: the original letter is the origin, the first letter of thinker

explanation.surface: A souvenir of a great thinker who had original ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'original' takes the first letter of 'thinker', T, after LOCKE.
explanation.definitionFit: A small hinged pendant holding a photograph or lock of hair is kept as a keepsake.

clue.text: Heraldic lion provides source for historians

indicators.note: the two words provide the answer from within their letters, across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A heraldic beast on a coat of arms serving as evidence for historians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'provides' signals the run spanning heraldiC LIOn. In Greek myth she is the Muse of history.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the Muse who inspires history, so writers of the past draw on her.

clue.text: Wind a string in, showing great skill

indicators.note: in puts the small pieces inside the wind

parts.note: the mistral is a cold northerly wind of southern France
on a violin the G-string is named by its note, so string gives G

explanation.surface: Someone winding a string skilfully into place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' reads as a verb (winding string) but is the noun MISTRAL; 'in' places A + G after its M.
explanation.definitionFit: Masterly or authoritative work is described with this word, from the Latin for master.

clue.text: It's unacceptable for 12 to take time

indicators.note: the midday word takes the time letter inside it

parts.note: twelve o'clock in the day is midday

explanation.surface: A complaint that the previous answer is taking too long.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' looks like a cross-reference to 12-across but is the number twelve, NOON; 'to take' puts T inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'that is not on' means it is not permissible or tolerable.

clue.text: Live in the present though retired

indicators.note: in places the living verb inside the present era

parts.note: AD, anno domini, marks the current era
to be is to exist, to live

explanation.surface: Advice to live in the moment despite being retired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' suggests stopping work, but here it means gone to bed; 'in' puts BE inside AD.
explanation.definitionFit: Having retired for the night means being tucked up in bed.

clue.text: Exclude what should be pocketed last

explanation.surface: Snooker advice about which ball to sink at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker the final colour potted is the black; to blackball is to vote someone out of a club.
explanation.definitionFit: Club members once barred candidates by casting a dark ball; in snooker the dark ball is potted at the finish.

clue.text: Frank pinched Bill's ham

indicators.note: pinched means squeezed between, holding the bill inside

parts.note: frank means open, overt
AC, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: Frank stealing a piece of ham belonging to Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' and 'Bill' look like names but are synonyms; 'pinched' looks like theft but places AC inside OVERT.
explanation.definitionFit: A ham actor performs with exaggerated gestures; to ham is to exaggerate on stage.

clue.text: Soft nose broken promptly in the past

indicators.note: broken signals the letters of soft nose are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: A soft nose broken quickly in some past incident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges SOFTNOSE. The answer is an archaic word, so the definition flags it as old.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Middle English adverb meaning soon afterwards, now obsolete, hence 'in the past'.

clue.text: Father of England opener? Quite the contrary

parts.note: the opposite of an opener is something that ends, a finisher

explanation.surface: Asking who fathered England's opening batsman, then reversing the idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite the contrary' flips 'opener' into its opposite, ENDER; 'opener' suggests a cricket batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: To father something is to beget or bring it into being, a verb sense.

clue.text: Stridently prejudiced source of entertainment

parts.note: F stands for forte, loud, the musical marking for strident playing
prejudiced treatment is biased, unfair

explanation.surface: A loud complaint about bias at a show.
explanation.walkthrough: F is the musical direction forte, meaning loudly.
explanation.definitionFit: A travelling fair with rides and stalls provides amusement for visitors.

clue.text: Musical figure for half the hoi polloi

indicators.note: half signals that only the first portion of the rabble word is kept

parts.note: ...-raff are the rabble, the common people

explanation.surface: A tune for half of the common masses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' keeps the front half of RIFFRAFF, a synonym for the hoi polloi.
explanation.definitionFit: A short repeated phrase in jazz or rock is a recurring melodic motif.

clue.text: Money man

explanation.surface: Two words linking cash and a chap.
explanation.definitionFit: The Deutschmark was former German currency; a boy's name, such as the gospel writer, gives the man.

clue.text: Trough containing a supervisor

indicators.note: containing places the letter inside the trough word

parts.note: a manger is a feeding trough for animals

explanation.surface: A feeding trough with a supervisor inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'containing' puts A inside MANGER after its first N.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss in charge of staff or an operation oversees work as its supervisor.

clue.text: The butt of the former governor of North Dakota

parts.note: the Doge was the elected ruler of Venice and Genoa in the past
ND is the US postal abbreviation for North Dakota

explanation.surface: Mocking a former governor of North Dakota as a laughing stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butt' suggests the target of a joke but means a cigarette end. DOGE is the old title of the ruler of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: The stub left after smoking a cigarette is called a butt.

clue.text: Stable-manager left store in disarray

indicators.note: in disarray means jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A stablehand who has left the store in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in disarray' scrambles L and STORE together.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn's groom looked after travellers' horses, managing the stable.

clue.text: Disturbed snake in the grass

indicators.note: disturbed means stirred up, so the letters of snake are moved about

explanation.surface: A snake agitated in long grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbed' rearranges SNAKE; the whole clue also defines, since a treacherous person is a snake in the grass.
explanation.definitionFit: A snake in the grass is a treacherous person, a furtive tell-tale.

clue.text: Works parties

explanation.surface: Two words: labour and celebrations.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine's operations are what it does when it works; formal receptions and dinners are social events, i.e. parties.

clue.text: Ivory river filling street up

indicators.note: filling means the river goes inside the street
in a down clue up means the piece is read bottom to top

parts.note: the Usk is a river in Wales

explanation.surface: Ivory carried up a street by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ST into TS, and 'filling' puts USK inside it. The USK is a Welsh river.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephant teeth are the source of ivory, standing as an example for the material.

clue.text: Trial of gold and wood

parts.note: or is the heraldic term for gold
deal is pine or fir timber

explanation.surface: A test involving gold and timber.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is gold in heraldry; DEAL is softwood planks.
explanation.definitionFit: A painful experience that tests endurance is a trial; medieval trial by ordeal is the origin.

clue.text: China encourages male students

parts.note: to egg on is to encourage
he is the male pronoun
L is a learner, so two Ls are students

explanation.surface: A Chinese figure encouraging male students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' reads as the country but is porcelain. L stands for learner, from the L-plates of British learner drivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Very thin delicate porcelain is called by this name for its fragile translucence.

clue.text: Beyond question ill-disposed to admit point

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the point goes inside

parts.note: surly means bad-tempered, ill-disposed
E, East, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone grumpy who certainly must concede a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to admit' puts E inside SURLY, after SUR.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb expresses certainty, meaning without doubt.

clue.text: Campaigner becomes less refined when back inside

indicators.note: inside places the reversed word within the other

parts.note: cruder means rougher, less refined

indicators.note: back signals the short word is turned round

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as he left'

explanation.surface: An activist turning coarser once returned home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns AS into SA, and 'inside' places it within CRUDER.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who fights vigorously for a cause is a reformer or activist; the word comes from holy war knights.
